name: XtraMath
line: XtraMath drills math facts as timed flashcards. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs XtraMath: XtraMath drills the facts of the four operations as adaptive flashcards. In AMP, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: XtraMath practices addition, subtraction, multiplication and division facts as an adaptive set of flashcards, each answered against a time limit, and its maker says it does not teach the strategies behind them [1][2][4]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous across all of math. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In XtraMath the unit is the fact, shown as a flashcard with a time limit [2][4]. Its maker says the program does not teach the strategies or concepts behind an operation [4]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [7].

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. XtraMath starts a new student with a placement quiz that usually spans two or three days, then sets the mix of facts from each student's strengths and weaknesses [2][4].

reasons.title: What counts as learned
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. In XtraMath a fact counts as fluent when it is answered correctly within its time limit, and a fluency score of 100 in one operation moves the student to the next [2][4].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP runs from counting through precalculus in one program, on one map of skills, and keeps a separate level for each part of math. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. XtraMath practices the facts of the four operations, plus fact programs a teacher defines, and brings in harder facts as a set becomes fluent [2][3].

rows.range: Math facts: addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, plus fact programs a teacher defines [1][3].
rows.start: A placement quiz across the four operations, which usually spans two or three days [2][3].
rows.teaching: None. Its maker describes adaptive flashcards and says the program does not teach the strategies or concepts behind an operation [4].
rows.next: A mix of facts set by each student's strengths and weaknesses. Harder facts arrive as a set becomes fluent [2][4].
rows.mastery: A fact is fluent when answered correctly within its time limit. A fluency score of 100 moves the student to the next operation [2][4].
rows.review: A two-minute quiz on earlier facts opens each session, and practice uses spaced repetition [2].
rows.print: Printable math and STEM activities. None made from one student's record found in the pages we read [3].
rows.adult: Creates accounts, chooses the program and the time limit, and reads the reports [1][2].
rows.reports: Accuracy, speed and fluency for each student and operation [1].
rows.evidence: Listed by Evidence for ESSA without a rating. No outcome study found on its site [1][5].

theirs: XtraMath calls its program a math fact fluency program: recall of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division facts, plus custom fact programs teachers define [1][3]. Its maker describes the program as an adaptive set of flashcards [4].

A new student starts with a placement quiz, which usually spans two or three days [2]. After that a session takes about ten minutes. It opens with a two-minute quiz on facts learned before, then two practice activities. Each fact has a time limit, shown as a moving bar, which teachers can lengthen or hide [2]. A fluency score of 100 in one operation moves the student to the next [4].
credit: Fast recall of the basic facts is its job. A What Works Clearinghouse practice guide rates regular timed activities to build fluency as strong evidence for elementary students who struggle in math [6].
Earlier facts come back at the start of every session, and practice uses spaced repetition [2].

theirs: XtraMath's home page calls the program "ESSA Tier IV certified" and reports that 96% of educators agree it helps students meet grade-level standards [1]. Tier IV is ESSA's rationale level: a stated logic for why a program should work, not a study of whether it did. The educator figure is a survey of opinion.
Evidence for ESSA lists XtraMath without a rating: "No studies met inclusion requirements" [5]. We found no outcome study on XtraMath's site.
ours: A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve mathematics performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 [7]. Every AMP problem carries a worked example in its lesson and a worked answer after it is answered.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: Your child knows how the four operations work and needs the facts to come quickly.
amp: You want one program from counting through precalculus, with a level for each part of math.
When your child misses something, you want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer right there.
You want a skill to count only when it is right without help, more than once.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice, mixed with other math.

questions.question: How is AMP different from XtraMath?
questions.answer: XtraMath practices the facts of the four operations as timed, adaptive flashcards, and its maker says it does not teach the strategies behind them [2][4]. AMP covers counting through precalculus. Every answer sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

questions.question: Does XtraMath work?
questions.answer: Evidence for ESSA lists XtraMath without a rating, because no studies met its inclusion requirements [5]. XtraMath cites ESSA Tier IV and an educator survey [1]. We found no outcome study on its site.

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
